Additionally, we observe that for some transformed coefficient distributions, and given the context adaptive binary arithmetic coding (CABAC) context, a small QP decrease may result in almost no rate increment. This can be explained by two facts. First, the CABAC context may be better suited when changing QP, making the entropy coding of quantized coefficients more efficient. Second, a slight quantized coefficient bitrate increase can be compensated by the differential QP syntax bitrate decrease. These two cases generate a lower rate than foreseen that we name “rate-drop.” Overall, refining locally a set of QP candidates can, at the same time, be beneficial for both rate and distortion, without compromising any global RDO, and that is what LQR does. Finally, thanks to additional heuristics and optimizations (e.g., distortion estimation in the transform domain), the LQR implementation can be kept reasonable in terms of computation overhead, with an overall encoding runtime increase measured below 10% in a MediaKind optimized software HEVC encoder. The compression efficiency performance of the LQR algorithm combined with STAQ (RDSTQ), implemented into ×265 and using JCT-VC common test conditions, is summarized in Table 3. Complementary to the STAQ algorithm, the coding efficiency advantage is about 6% bitrate saving for the same PSNR- or SSIMbased quality. Conclusion By sharing an overview of the hybrid video coding scheme that holds for most modern video compression standards, we highlight the key role of the quantization in optimizing the video quality/bitrate tradeoff, as the (almost) only adjustable lossy processing step in any encoding system. We consequently detail the various levels of granularity and control points available for quantization optimization, most notably the block or CU-level QP adaptation. As practical examples, we introduce and share some insights on two differentiating quantization algorithms, namely STAQ and LQR.
